title: Gymkhana's Kitchen Goes Retail: Michelin-Starred Indian Sauces Land at Whole Foods
excerpt: The London restaurant group behind eight Michelin stars raises $8.5 million to bring its simmer sauces to American home kitchens, marking what insiders call Indian food's 'premium moment.'
body:
When Karam Sethi and his siblings Jyotin and Sunaina opened Gymkhana in London's Mayfair thirteen years ago, they had one ambition: to prove that Indian food belonged at the highest table in global gastronomy. The restaurant earned a Michelin star. Then the Sethi family's JKS Restaurants group earned seven more, across a portfolio of more than thirty concepts. Now, Gymkhana is asking a bolder question — can that same kitchen credibility travel from a white-tablecloth dining room to a Whole Foods shelf?

The answer, apparently, is yes, and it comes with $8.5 million in backing.

## From Fine Dining to the Grocery Aisle

Gymkhana Fine Foods, the consumer-packaged-goods arm of the restaurant brand, has launched nationally at Whole Foods Market stores across the United States. The product line includes simmer sauces and marinades — butter masala, Goan coconut curry, korma, tikka masala, madras, classic tandoori barbecue, green tikka, and roasted garlic and chili — priced between $8 and $10 per jar.

The launch is powered by a Series A funding round led by CAVU Consumer Partners, co-founded by Rohan Oza, the investor and "Shark Tank" personality whose portfolio includes Poppi, Bai, and Vital Proteins. Jared Jacobs, managing partner at CAVU, and Oza will continue to serve on the company's board.

"This isn't just a product launch — it's the beginning of Indian food's premium moment in America," said Gulrez Singh Arora, CEO and co-founder of Gymkhana Fine Foods. The statement is deliberate. Indian food has long had a presence in American grocery stores through brands like Patak's, Maya Kaimal, and Deep Indian Kitchen. But Gymkhana is betting that the market is ready for something positioned explicitly at the premium end — restaurant-grade, Michelin-credentialed, and unapologetically full-flavored.

## The Sethi Playbook: Restaurants First, Then Retail

The CPG launch follows a strategic pattern. Last year, JKS opened the first US Gymkhana restaurant at the Aria Resort & Casino in Las Vegas. Earlier this year, the group debuted Ambassadors Clubhouse, a Punjabi-inspired concept, in New York. Eight Michelin stars and six Bib Gourmand mentions across the group's global portfolio give the brand a halo that few competitors in the Indian sauce aisle can match.

In the UK, Gymkhana Fine Foods launched in 2023 at Whole Foods stores across London, backed by a $3 million seed round also led by CAVU. The US launch is the natural next step, and the choice of Whole Foods as the exclusive retail partner signals a clear positioning: this is not a mass-market play for the ethnic food shelf. It is a bid for the premium sauce aisle, alongside brands like Rao's and Momofuku.

Karam Sethi, who serves as culinary and creative director for JKS, described the move as a natural extension of the restaurant's founding mission. "Each sauce, marinade, and chutney has been created to deliver the same bold, authentic flavors found in our restaurants," he said.

## Indian Cuisine's Investment Moment

Gymkhana's fundraise is part of a broader trend. Last year, private equity firm L Catterton invested in Dishoom, another acclaimed London-based Indian restaurant group that is reportedly eyeing US expansion. Indian food brands are attracting institutional capital at a rate unseen even five years ago. The global Indian food market, driven partly by diaspora demand and partly by mainstream curiosity, is maturing rapidly.

For Indian Americans, the news carries a particular resonance. Generations of NRIs have watched "curry" be treated as a catch-all term for an entire cuisine's diversity, watched Indian food sit in the ethnic aisle while Italian and Japanese products were mainstreamed, and watched Michelin guides largely overlook Indian restaurants. That landscape is shifting — and Gymkhana's bet is that the American home cook is ready to shift with it.

## What's in the Jar

The sauces are developed from recipes used at the restaurant. The butter masala uses a slow-cooked tomato and cashew base. The Goan coconut curry leans into the coastal flavours of Konkan. The tandoori barbecue marinade is designed for grilling. Each jar is meant to serve as a complete cooking sauce — add protein or vegetables, simmer, and serve.

Whether a $9 jar of Gymkhana masala can compete with the $3.69 Tasty Bite pouch or the $4.99 Maya Kaimal dal is a question the market will answer. But the play is not about price — it is about repositioning Indian food in the same premium category that once seemed reserved for Italian and French cuisine. If a jar of Rao's marinara can command $8.99 and become a cultural phenomenon, Gymkhana is asking: why not butter masala?

For Indian Americans who have always known that their grandmother's masala was worth more than the ethnic aisle implied, the answer has been obvious for a long time. Gymkhana is simply putting a price tag on what the diaspora already knew.
